Business profit is not cash ready for the household: follow stock, unpaid invoices and owner withdrawals

Trace a cash inventory purchase and a credit sale through operating profit, customer collection and a proposed owner withdrawal, including funding gaps hidden by a positive month-end balance.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow a cash inventory purchase, a credit sale and one proposed owner withdrawal

Interactive planning lab

Modeled operating profit from the one sale$12,000
Projected cash just before the proposed withdrawal$6,000
Extra opening owner cash needed for the requested calendar$6,000

Original hypothetical six-month business cash plan, not financial statements or a salary/dividend/tax calculation. A batch is purchased for cash at the start of month one; half is delivered and invoiced at the start of month two. That half’s original cost is recognized once as cost of goods sold; the remaining half stays at original cost, without a market valuation or impairment assessment. One operating expense is recognized and paid alongside the sale. The whole customer invoice is assumed collected after opening expenses in its entered month. The one owner withdrawal follows any same-month collection and is a transfer, not an operating expense. Other months have no new sales or operating costs. Negative requested cash balances are unmet funding requirements, not approved overdrafts or completed unfunded payments. The separately shown opening top-up is the amount that would be needed from outside owner cash before events begin; its availability is not assumed proven. No supplier credit, loans, interest, bad debts, inventory resale, sales tax or income tax is modeled. End-of-month and ordered-event views retain different timing detail.

The central idea

Profit, business assets and withdrawable cash are different amounts. Match an owner transfer to collected cash and the business’s payment calendar before using it in a household budget.

01

Start with the business transactions before assigning money to the household

A business owner can record a profitable sale before the customer pays. The household may see that profit as available income even while the business has already used cash to buy stock and still needs money for operating bills.

BDC’s cash-flow explanation distinguishes receipts and payments from revenue and costs. Its cash-conversion discussion also identifies inventory and customer receivables as places where money can remain tied up. This guide uses those general distinctions in an independently authored example.

The model follows one inventory batch, one sale, one operating expense and one proposed owner transfer over six months. It is a cash-planning illustration, rather than formal financial statements or a determination of salary, dividend or taxable income. All amounts and dates are hypothetical, and the customer is assumed to pay the full invoice.

02

The full inventory purchase uses cash before all of it becomes an expense

The default business opens with CAD 20,000 of cash. At the start of month one, it purchases a CAD 12,000 batch for cash. The bank balance falls to CAD 8,000, while inventory at original cost rises to CAD 12,000. The purchase has moved value between two business assets; no sale has yet produced profit.

Half of the batch is delivered and invoiced in month two for CAD 20,000. The cost attached to that half is CAD 6,000. The other half remains in inventory at its CAD 6,000 original cost. A separate CAD 2,000 operating expense is recognized and paid alongside the sale.

The modeled operating profit is therefore CAD 20,000 of revenue minus CAD 6,000 of sold-stock cost minus CAD 2,000 of operating expense, or CAD 12,000. Deducting the full batch purchase from profit and then also deducting the sold half would count inventory cost twice. Remaining stock is not valued at an assumed resale profit, and no impairment or formal reporting assessment is made.

03

An unpaid invoice does not fund the requested owner withdrawal

The customer’s CAD 20,000 invoice is collected in month three under the default timing. In month two, the business instead holds a receivable for that amount. Paying the CAD 2,000 operating cost reduces bank cash from CAD 8,000 to CAD 6,000, even though the sale has generated CAD 12,000 of modeled profit.

The proposed owner withdrawal is also CAD 12,000 and is scheduled after other events in month two. Only CAD 6,000 is projected before that transfer. The requested calendar therefore has a CAD 6,000 funding gap. A negative cash line identifies that unmet requirement; it is not an approved overdraft or evidence that the withdrawal can actually be made.

Delaying the same transfer until month three would, under these exact assumptions, place it after customer collection. That timing change removes the default gap without changing operating profit. It does not establish that a customer will pay as expected, or that the household can postpone its own bills until then.

04

Reconcile the month-two bank balance without subtracting costs twice

The second waterfall starts with the original CAD 20,000 of cash and adds CAD 12,000 of operating profit. It then subtracts the CAD 20,000 uncollected invoice, CAD 6,000 still held as stock and CAD 12,000 of proposed owner withdrawals through that checkpoint.

The result is negative CAD 6,000, matching the requested cash calendar. The inventory and receivable adjustments explain why the profit total did not translate into money available in the bank. The owner transfer reduces business cash but is kept separate from operating profit in this illustration.

The identified opening funding requirement is CAD 6,000. The funded asset chart assumes that exact amount is contributed by the owner before the transactions begin. It does not treat the contribution as a new sale or additional profit. Such money must come from somewhere outside this business plan and may already have a purpose in the household budget.

05

Check the order of payments instead of relying only on the closing balance

The cash chart uses ordered event checkpoints. The spacing is deliberately chronological rather than a scale of elapsed months, and the data table gives each event’s month and description. Operating payments come before customer collection; an owner withdrawal comes after any collection in the same month.

Try a separate scenario with CAD 5,000 of opening cash, no owner withdrawal and customer collection in month two. Buying the CAD 12,000 stock first leaves a CAD 7,000 deficit. Paying the CAD 2,000 operating cost before collection increases that requirement to CAD 9,000. The later CAD 20,000 receipt produces positive closing cash of CAD 11,000.

Looking only at that positive month-end amount would miss the earlier funding need. The model therefore computes its opening contribution from the minimum across ordered events, rather than monthly closing balances alone. It makes the requirement visible without assuming that a lender or the household will supply the money.

06

Keep the remaining business assets and next cycle out of today’s household spending

After the default proposed withdrawal and eventual customer collection, the requested plan ends with CAD 14,000 of bank cash and CAD 6,000 of remaining inventory. Adding the identified CAD 6,000 opening contribution would instead leave CAD 20,000 of cash plus that same stock. The larger funded balance reflects new owner capital, rather than stronger operating performance.

The date matrix changes collection and withdrawal months while keeping every amount selected. There are no new recurring costs after month two in this simple example. A later collection can therefore lengthen a funding gap without increasing its peak size. A real business with continuing rent, payroll or stock purchases needs those payments added to its schedule.

The remaining stock is an asset at original cost, not money that can automatically be removed. Receivables, taxes, future purchases and existing earmarks also need separate attention before an owner transfer funds personal spending. The sales-tax reserve guide covers another distinction between bank cash and money available to keep. Use the business cash calendar and household budget together, while preserving the difference between earned profit, external funding and an actual transfer.
